message:
CALL GOAL: Expand Logatlas from Tessera's core payments estate to the newly acquired merchant-lending business (est. 40 new log sources).

OPEN
"Mei-Lin, Rutger from Logatlas. You mentioned on the QBR that the lending acquisition closes this month. I've got a couple of questions about their data. Ten minutes?"

WHY NOW
"When we onboarded your core estate, Logatlas found 23 log sources your detection team assumed were parsed correctly but weren't, mostly timestamp and user-field problems. That's what let your team trust the AI-assisted rule drafts.

Lending is coming over with its own logging conventions, built by a different team, and from what I've heard it's not well documented."

QUESTIONS
- "What's the plan for their logs: onboard into your SIEM as-is, or normalize first?"
- "Who knows their data today? Is that person staying?"
- "Your detection agents read Logatlas to understand field names. What happens when they hit lending data that isn't mapped?"

[Key point: unmapped data means the agents will guess, or skip. Let her get there herself.]

PROPOSAL
"I'd suggest mapping the lending sources before they go into production detections. About 40 sources, roughly three weeks. You'd get field maps, sample events and a taxonomy that matches your existing one, so rules written for payments can be extended to lending without rewriting."

PRICING POSITION
"It's an extension of your current subscription, priced per source, co-termed to your renewal. I'll send numbers after this call."

HANDLE "WE'LL DO IT MANUALLY"
"You could. Your team did that for the first payments sources and it took about four months, by your estimate. The bigger risk is that the person who knows lending's data leaves during the integration."

CLOSE
"Can we get the lending infrastructure lead on a call next week so I can see what they're sending?"
quality_notes: Times the expansion to an acquisition trigger and uses a concrete prior result (23 misparsed sources) as proof. Guides the buyer to realize unmapped data will undermine their detection agents, and the manual-effort objection is handled with their own history.

message:
GOAL: Expand Crossover from the completed SIEM migration to the planned move of long-tail detections into the data lake.

OPEN
"Theodric, Annelise from Crossover. I saw the architecture review deck you shared with our team, the one with the data lake tiering plan. Do you have a few minutes to talk about the detection side of it?"

CONTEXT
"Last year Crossover moved 1,800 rules onto your current SIEM. In the new plan, about 40% of your data, mainly network flow and DNS, moves to the data lake to save cost. Which means a chunk of your detections now need to run in a different query engine, against different table structures."

QUESTIONS
- "Have you sized how many detections touch the data moving to the lake?"
- "Who's going to rewrite them? Your detection engineers or the data platform team?"
- "How will you know a rewritten rule actually behaves the same as the original?"

[That last question is the key. Last time, validation against live data is what caught 210 rules that would have broken silently.]

POSITION
"Crossover can run the same process again, but with the lake as the target: translate each affected rule, run it side by side against the same time window in both places, and flag any that return different results. Your team only reviews the exceptions."

ESTIMATE
"From the deck, I'd guess 300 to 400 affected rules. Validation is where most of the time goes, so I'd plan on six to eight weeks."

HANDLE "THE DATA PLATFORM TEAM WILL HANDLE IT"
"They may well be great at moving data. Ask them how they'll prove the detections still fire. If they've got an answer, great. If not, we're a call away."

CLOSE
"Could I get 45 minutes with you and the data platform lead to map out which rules are affected? That alone will tell you whether you need us."
quality_notes: Anchors the expansion in the customer's own architecture plan and the prior migration's validation results. The questions surface the real risk (proving rewritten rules still fire), and the close offers a scoping session that has value even if they don't buy.

message:

It also tracks analyst hours saved, which is useful when you're asking for headcount and someone asks what you did with the last hire.

Manufacturers we work with usually find that their top ten noisiest rules make up about half their total alert volume, so even a little tuning goes a long way.

I'd love to set up a call to learn more about your SOC and see if this could help. You can reply to the email or grab time with the link below.

Thanks Victor, and good luck with the alert queue today.
quality_notes: Good empathetic opening with plausible manufacturing-specific noise examples, but it's a standard cold pitch with an unspecific call ask and an unverified 'about half' claim instead of an offer to look at his actual rules.

message:
Good afternoon, Hamid. This is Elodie Fontaine with Crossover. Thank you for joining our roundtable on SIEM migration at the Mid-Atlantic Public Sector Cyber Summit.

You shared that your department is under a mandate to move to the state's shared SIEM platform by the end of next fiscal year, and that you have about 900 detection rules, many written by contractors who are no longer engaged. You also said your biggest fear is not the migration itself, but discovering six months later that a third of the rules translated without errors and simply never fire.

That concern is well founded. Rule translation is the easy part. The difficult part is that field names, data models, and log source coverage differ between platforms, so a rule can be syntactically correct and functionally blind.

[Screen: blurred validation report]

Crossover addresses this by validating each translated rule against live data in the target platform. For every rule, you receive one of four results: validated and firing as expected, translated but missing required telemetry, translated with field mapping issues, or not translatable and requiring redesign. That gives your team a defensible inventory to bring to the oversight committee.

Given public procurement timelines, I would propose a modest first step: a migration readiness assessment on a sample of 100 rules, conducted under your existing cooperative purchasing agreement so it does not require a new solicitation. The results would give you a realistic estimate of effort for the full library.

I will follow this video with an email summarizing the assessment scope. If it would be helpful, I am glad to brief your deputy director as well. Thank you, Hamid.
buyer_reply: This is helpful. Please send the scope and confirm the cooperative agreement number so I can check it with our contracts office.
quality_notes: Formal tone suits a public-sector buyer; it restates his mandate and specific fear, explains the risk credibly, and proposes a procurement-aware first step that avoids a new solicitation.

message:

message:

quality_notes: Wrong persona and wrong framing: pitches a CFO on technical health-check jargon and a price without the security team's sponsorship, risk quantification, or a business case she'd recognize.

message:
[Seller in front of a whiteboard with a hand-drawn grid]

Hi Charlotte, Aurelio from Coverwise. We spoke at the booth at HarborSec on Thursday, right before the closing keynote.

You told me something I've heard from a lot of architects but rarely so bluntly: your coverage map says you're at about seventy percent of the techniques that matter to you, and you don't believe it. Your reasoning was that the map counts rules, not rules that actually work against the data you have.

[Taps the grid]

You're right to be suspicious. Here's the difference in how Coverwise counts. A technique only shows as covered if three things are true: there's a detection mapped to it, that detection is healthy and has run successfully recently, and the log sources it depends on are actually flowing into your SIEM at the volume you'd expect. If any of those fail, it shows as "claimed but unproven," in a different color, so you can see the gap between what the spreadsheet says and what's real.

In our experience with life sciences companies, the gap is usually biggest in two places: lab instrument networks, where telemetry is spotty, and research data exfiltration, where rules exist but depend on cloud storage logs that were never fully onboarded.

[Back to camera]

What I'd propose is simple. Give us read-only access for a week, and we'll produce your real map alongside your current one. If the numbers match, you've validated your board metric, which is worth something. If they don't, you'll know exactly where to look.

quality_notes: Restates the architect's skepticism in her own terms, explains precisely how the product's counting differs, adds industry-specific insight, and offers a proof with value whatever the outcome.

message:

message:
Graham, Odalys from Logatlas. Two minutes, one question.

When a detection engineer on your team wants to write a rule against your core banking authentication logs, where do they go to find out what fields exist, what the values look like, and whether that log source is even complete?

[Pause]

If the answer is "they ask Graham," that's the problem we solve.

In most banks I talk to, the knowledge of what data actually exists in the SIEM lives in two or three people's heads, plus a wiki page someone updated in 2023. Every time a log source changes, a vendor updates a format, or a new team onboards a source, that knowledge drifts. And now that teams are pointing AI agents at their SIEM to help write detections, those agents have the same problem, except they're more confident about guessing wrong.

[Screen: blurred Logatlas page for one log source]

Logatlas builds and maintains a living data dictionary for every log source: fields with types and example values, sample events, event categories, how complete the source is over time, and a normalized taxonomy across sources. It refreshes automatically, so when your authentication log format changes, you see it the same week, not the next time a detection breaks.

It's useful for humans and for agents, and it means you stop being the human index.

[Back to camera]

If this sounds familiar, I'd suggest a 30-minute look where we generate the dictionary for three of your log sources live. You'd keep the output. Reply to the email this came in, and I'll set it up.
quality_notes: Opens with a pointed question that makes the buyer the hero, uses a memorable line ('stop being the human index'), adds a timely AI-agent angle, and offers a concrete live proof where he keeps the output.

message:
Hi Hannah, Emeka from Signalcraft. In your last email you said, totally fairly, that your team already gets plenty of detection content from the open community repositories and your EDR vendor's built-in rules, so you don't see why you'd pay for more.

I want to respond properly, because I agree with part of that.

The community content is great, and you should keep using it. The question isn't whether you have access to detections. It's how long it takes your team to make each one actually work in your environment. You mentioned in our first call that Torvald runs a pretty customized SIEM after the merger with the parts division: custom field extractions for the dealer network, macros your team built for the manufacturing plants, and a few data models that don't follow the standard naming.

Every community rule your team imports has to be adapted to all of that. Field names changed, macros swapped in, lookups wired up, tested. In most customized environments that's anywhere from an hour to a full day per rule. That's the cost Signalcraft removes. It reads your existing customizations first and writes or adapts detections to use them, the way your engineers would.

[Screen: side-by-side of a generic rule and an adapted rule, blurred]

So I'm not suggesting you replace your sources. I'm suggesting a test. Pick five community rules your team wants but hasn't had time to adapt. We'll run them through Signalcraft, your engineers review the output, and you measure how much time it saved. If the answer is "not much," I'll stop bringing it up.

Sound fair? Just reply with the five, or reply "not now" and I'll check back next quarter.
buyer_reply: Fair enough. I have a backlog of about 30 we never got to. I'll send five, the ugliest ones.
quality_notes: Acknowledges the objection as partly right, reframes the cost from content access to adaptation time using the buyer's own environment details, and proposes a measurable test with an easy opt-out.

message:

message:

quality_notes: Uses the referral well with a credible peer metric and telco-specific insight, but it drifts into a general product pitch and leaves the next step loose instead of proposing a specific time or advisory.

message:
Hi Gideon, it's Rafaela from Tunebench. You were on our webinar about alert fatigue last Thursday, and you dropped a comment in the chat that I haven't stopped thinking about. You wrote: "We have six analysts and they each have a private list of alerts they ignore."

That's one of the most honest things I've heard a SOC manager say, and it's far more common than people admit. It's not laziness. When a rule fires hundreds of times a week and has never once been a real incident, people build their own coping mechanisms. The problem is that six private ignore lists means six different versions of what your SOC is actually watching.

[Screen: blurred Tunebench rule analysis]

Here's what Tunebench would do with that. Instead of each analyst silently ignoring a rule, Tunebench looks at the rule's history, explains what's driving the noise, for a bank your size it's often things like core banking batch jobs or a vendor's remote support tool, and proposes a specific exclusion or threshold change. Your team reviews it, approves it, and it's documented. So the ignore list becomes a tuning decision everyone can see, with a record of why.

The other thing it does is track hours saved, which tends to help when you're explaining to leadership why six analysts is not enough, or why it actually is.

[Back to camera]

So here's an idea. Ask each of your six analysts to write down their top three ignored alerts. That's a fifteen-minute exercise, and it's useful even if you never talk to me again. If the lists overlap the way I suspect they will, send me the top five, and we'll show you what Tunebench recommends for each one.

Thanks, Gideon. And thanks for saying the quiet part in the chat.
quality_notes: Builds the whole message on the buyer's own chat comment, reframes it without judgment, explains the product through his situation, and suggests an exercise that's useful even without buying.

message:

[Screen: blurred multi-team board]

Commonground gives you one shared backlog across all of those teams without forcing them to give up their own workflow. quality_notes: Respects her travel schedule with an async format, recalls her own phrasing, reframes the issue as a program problem that fits a CISO, and gives a specific, scoped ask with a named stakeholder.

message:
Moses, Annelise from Quietwatch. We talked for about ten minutes at the booth at the Desert SecOps Symposium, and you told me a story I want to repeat back to you, because it's the whole reason this product exists.

Last year your team found out, during a tabletop exercise, that the detection for unauthorized changes to your crew scheduling system hadn't fired in eleven months. Not because nothing happened, but because the application team moved the logs to a new index during an upgrade and nobody told the SOC. If any of those answers change, it tells you, with the root cause and a proposed fix.

[Screen: blurred list of silent detections with categories]

For an airline, I'd want to start with the detections tied to operationally critical systems. Crew scheduling, flight ops, maintenance records, the reservation platform. Those are the ones where silent failure has real-world consequences.

So my ask is this: a read-only health scan of your detection library, with a focus on those systems. One day of setup, and you get the report whether or not you buy anything. If it comes back clean, you've got proof for your auditors. If it doesn't, you've found the next crew scheduling problem before the tabletop does.

buyer_reply: Funny timing. Our auditors asked last week how we know our critical detections work. Send the details, I'll get our SIEM engineer on it.
quality_notes: Retells the buyer's own near-miss as the anchor, delivers a crisp line ('find the next one on purpose'), maps the product to airline-critical systems, and offers a read-only scan with value regardless of purchase.

message:
Hi Yasmin, Marcel from Coverwise. I've reached out a few times since we met at the Ironbridge Security Forum, and I haven't heard back, which usually means one of three things: the timing is wrong, the problem isn't a priority, or my emails are landing somewhere between a phishing simulation and the spam folder.

Any of those is fine. This will be my last message for now.

Just to leave you with something useful: when we spoke, you mentioned that your coverage reporting for the plant networks was mostly based on what rules exist, not on whether the operational technology telemetry those rules need is actually being collected. If you ever want a quick way to sanity check that, pick five of your OT-related detections and look at when their underlying log sources last sent data. That check takes about an hour and it usually tells you whether a deeper coverage review is worth doing. In my experience, at plants that grew through acquisitions, at least one of those five sources has been quiet for months, usually because a historian server or a firewall was replaced and the forwarding config never got rebuilt. Nobody's fault, it just happens when the OT and IT teams have separate change processes.

If you ever do want to go deeper, Coverwise can automate that check for every technique in your threat model. My details are in the email. Thanks, Yasmin, and good luck with the plant rollouts.
quality_notes: Graceful breakup that leaves behind a practical self-check tied to her situation, but at over two minutes it's longer than a breakup needs, and the humor about spam folders slightly undercuts the professional tone.

message:
Hey Rohan, it's Delphine from Baseline Forge. We had a demo booked at the booth at DetectCon East on Wednesday, and I'm guessing the incident your pager went off for during the morning keynote ate the rest of your day. I hope it turned out to be minor.

Since we didn't get to the demo, I'll give you the version I would have shown you, in about three minutes.

You told me when we booked it that your biggest gap is around insider-type behavior in your production environment: engineers with legitimate access doing something unusual. Static rules don't help much there, because almost everything those engineers do is technically allowed.

[Screen: blurred baseline view]

Here's how Baseline Forge approaches it. First, it builds peer groups automatically, say, everyone on the data platform team versus everyone on the payments team. Then it baselines behavior per peer group: what production systems they touch, what volume of data they read, what hours they work. When someone drifts far outside their own history and their peer group's, you get a single, risk-scored alert with the explanation attached, rather than ten low-confidence alerts.

It all runs as scheduled searches in your SIEM, with state stored in lookups, so it's inspectable. You can see exactly why it scored something the way it did. For a principal engineer, I suspect that's the part you'd care about most.

[Back to camera]

If this is still on your list, I'd love to rebook the demo with your actual peer groups instead of our sample data. Just reply with a couple of times. And if the incident is still going, ignore this entirely and go get some sleep.
quality_notes: Handles a no-show with empathy and a plausible reason, delivers the missed demo's core value async, ties it to the gap the buyer himself named, and emphasizes inspectability for a technical persona.

message:

message:

message:

message:

quality_notes: Opens with outcomes the VP already cares about, uses QBR evidence to show a specific remaining gap, ties the upsell to her board narrative, and gives a scoped proposal with an easy out.

message:

message:

message:
[Dial. Pause after she answers.]

Hi Priyanka, it's Gabe Moreau with Signalcraft. This is a cold call, so I'll be honest about that. Can I take 30 seconds to tell you why I picked up the phone, and you tell me if it's worth another two minutes?

[If yes:]

Thanks. I talk to detection engineering leads at big media companies, and the thing I keep hearing is that public detection content doesn't survive contact with their SIEM. Every rule someone shares assumes field names and macros that don't exist in a studio's environment, so your team spends more time adapting rules than writing them. Is that true at Lanternfish, or have you already solved it?

[Listen. Likely answers:]

- "Yes, constantly." Ask: "Roughly what share of a new detection's time goes into adapting it to your naming, lookups and data models versus the actual logic?" Then: "Signalcraft writes the detection in your own query dialect, using your existing macros and lookups, so the draft runs on day one. Would it be useful to see it take one of your backlog items and draft it against your environment?"

- "We built our own conventions and tooling." Say: "That makes sense for a team your size. Where does it break down? New log sources, new hires learning the conventions, or the backlog itself?" Follow her answer; don't pitch until she names a pain.

- "Not a priority." Say: "Fair. What is the priority for detection engineering this quarter?" If it's not something we touch, thank her and ask if you can check back after planning season.

[Ask:]

"Here's what I'd suggest: a 25-minute working session where you bring one detection you've been meaning to write, and we show you the draft Signalcraft produces in your dialect. If it's not better than what your team would produce, you've lost 25 minutes and I'll stop calling. Fair?"

[If yes:] Lock a time on the call and confirm by email with the one detection she plans to bring. [If no:] "Understood. Mind if I send a two-line note so you have my name if the backlog grows?" Thank her and hang up.
quality_notes: Strong: asks permission, opens with a specific pain (public content not surviving a customized SIEM) framed as a question, branches on her answer and ties the ask to one real backlog detection with a clear exit. Compared with the weak version it listens before pitching and never forces the calendar invite.

message:
[Screen share from the start. Small webcam bubble in the corner.]

Tomasz, Nadia from Baseline Forge. Two minutes, one chart, and then I'll get out of your way.

[Show chart: weekly alert count for an impossible-travel style rule, anonymized sample data shaped like an insurer's.]

On our call last week you said your impossible-travel rule fires about 900 times a week, mostly from claims adjusters who log in from hotels, field sites and their phones within the same hour. You've been tuning it with a static allow-list, and the list is now longer than the rule.

Here's what the same logic looks like as a peer-group baseline. Instead of one global threshold, Baseline Forge learns what normal travel looks like for each peer group: field adjusters, underwriters, the call center. Then it scores logins against their own group's history.

[Highlight the drop.] On this sample, weekly alerts drop from about 900 to about 60, and the six real anomalies we planted are all still in the top 20 by risk score.

[Switch to the generated detection.] This is the scheduled search it would deploy in your environment. It uses your existing identity lookup and the risk-scoring fields your team already writes to, so it doesn't introduce a parallel pipeline you'd have to maintain.

Two caveats, because you'll ask: the baseline needs about 30 days of history to settle, and peer groups are only as good as your HR department data, which you mentioned is a bit messy for contractors.

My suggestion: send me two weeks of anonymized login events for one region, and we'll return this same chart built on your data, plus the query. If the numbers don't hold up, you'll know quickly and it costs you nothing but an export.

I'll follow up by email with the field list we'd need. Thanks, Tomasz.
quality_notes: Strong: uses the video to show his own named problem (a 900-a-week impossible-travel rule) solved as a peer-group baseline, states caveats a principal engineer would raise, and ends with a concrete low-cost test on his data. The weak version used the same format for company history.

message:
[Context: Russell has just said, "Honestly, we're planning to migrate the rules ourselves. We have smart people and a year to do it."]

[If he pushes back:] I'm not saying your team isn't smart. It's just that Crossover was built specifically for this. We've done dozens of migrations, and we have proprietary translation technology that handles all the edge cases. Your team would be starting from scratch.

[If he mentions budget:] I totally get budget is tight in government. But if you think about it, the cost of Crossover is way less than the cost of your team's time. Plus, if the migration goes wrong, you could be left with gaps in your detection coverage, and that's a big risk for a state agency. You don't want to be in the news.

[If he says he needs to think about it:] Of course. But I'd really encourage you not to wait too long, because our implementation calendar is filling up for next year and I can't guarantee we'll have capacity if you wait. Can we at least schedule a call with your CIO next week to walk through the business case?

[If he says no:] Okay, no problem. I'll send you some materials and follow up next week. I really think you're going to regret going it alone, but I respect your decision.

[Close:] Thanks Russell, talk soon.
quality_notes: Weak: answers the build-versus-buy objection by telling a security architect his plan is a bad idea, uses fear ('you'll be in the news') and capacity-scarcity pressure, and tries to escalate over his head to the CIO. It never asks how his team plans to do the migration.

message:
[Context: Russell has just said, "Honestly, we're planning to migrate the rules ourselves. We have smart people and a year to do it."]

Imani: That's a reasonable plan, and a lot of teams do it in-house. Can I ask a few questions about how you're thinking about it? If at the end it's clearly the right call to build, I'll tell you that.

[Ask, and take notes on each:]

1. "How many rules are in scope, and how many of those are custom versus shipped content?"
2. "How are you planning to validate that each translated rule actually fires on the new platform, not just that it parses?"
3. "Who on your team knows the old macros and lookups best, and what happens to the project if they're out for a month?"
4. "Are you running both SIEMs in parallel during the move? For how long?"

[Listen for: validation plan is vague; a key person dependency; a parallel-run period that's expensive.]

[If validation is vague:] "That's the part we see take the longest. Translating syntax is maybe a third of the work. The rest is proving each rule still catches what it caught before when the field names and data models are different. Crossover runs every translated rule against live data on both sides and flags the ones that will break, with the reason."

[If parallel run is long:] "Every month you run both platforms, you're paying twice for ingest. If we shorten the parallel run even by two months, that usually covers a large part of the cost."

[If he still prefers in-house:] "Then here's a middle path. Your team keeps ownership. We run Crossover's validation on a sample of 50 of your hardest rules, and your team uses the report however you like. You'll know quickly whether translation or validation is the real bottleneck."

[Close:] "Would it help if I sent the four questions in writing so you can run them past your team? And if the sample makes sense, we can scope it for your procurement process, including the cooperative purchasing contract you mentioned."

[Do not push for a CIO meeting. Let Russell decide who else joins.]
quality_notes: Strong: treats building in-house as legitimate, uses four diagnostic questions to find the real risk (validation, key-person dependency, double ingest cost) and offers a 50-rule sample that leaves ownership with his team. The weak version argued and applied fear; this one respects the architect and his process.

[Prep: on discovery, Kwame said Ironvale manages 85 client tenants, his team of six detection engineers keeps a separate copy of each rule per client, and a recent detection fix took nine days to roll out to everyone.]

[Dial.]

Yusuf: Kwame, Yusuf from Relaykit. I've got one specific thing for you, it'll take three minutes. Is now okay?

[If yes:]

Yusuf: On our first call you said a fix to the encoded-PowerShell-style detection took nine days to reach all 85 tenants because each client has its own copy and its own field names. I asked our SE to model what that rollout would look like in Relaykit using the three client environments you described: the healthcare group, the two manufacturers, and the credit union.

[Pause. Ask:] Does that match how you'd want the rollout to work, or is there a step your team does that I'm missing?

[Listen. If he raises client data separation:] Good question. Each tenant's data stays in its own environment. Relaykit only sends queries and reads results; nothing is pooled across clients. I can send the architecture diagram your clients' auditors usually ask for.

[If he raises cost per tenant:] Pricing is per tenant with tiers, and I'll bring numbers for 85 and 120 tenants since you mentioned the growth target.

Success means a detection fix rolls out to all five in under an hour, with failures explained. Can we get your lead engineer on a 30-minute scoping call this week?

[If yes:] Book it live. [If not yet:] Ask: "What would need to be true for this to be worth a pilot?" and write down the answer.
quality_notes: Strong: comes back with work done on Kwame's own scenario (a nine-day fix rollout across 85 tenants), reports a real result including a failure the buyer would care about, anticipates MSSP-specific objections, and proposes a pilot with a measurable success criterion. message:
[Context: Bettina has just said, "Look, I like it, but there's no budget this year. Our security spend got frozen after the booking-system project ran over."]

Cassius: That's clear, and thanks for telling me straight. I won't try to talk you around a freeze. Can I ask two questions so I know what to do with my time and yours?

1. "When does the freeze lift, or when does next year's budget get decided?"
2. "When it does, what will your CFO want to see before approving anything new in security?"

[Listen. Typical answers: planning in February; CFO wants hard savings or reduced risk tied to an incident.]

Cassius: That helps. Here's what I'd suggest, and none of it costs you anything.

Between now and February, we run Tunebench's analysis on your three noisiest rules, read-only. You told me the guest-Wi-Fi authentication rule alone generates around 1,200 alerts a week across the resorts. The output is a report: which alerts are noise, the tuning we'd propose, and the analyst hours it would free up, measured on your data, not our calculator.

If the numbers are small, you've learned that tuning isn't your problem and you can spend February's budget elsewhere. If they're big, you walk into planning with your own evidence.

[If she worries about effort:] "It's about an hour from your SIEM engineer to grant read-only access, and a 30-minute readout. That's it."

[If she asks what's in it for us:] "Fair question. If the report is compelling, I'd like to be in the February conversation. If it isn't, I'd rather know now."

[Close:] "Should I send a one-paragraph description of the analysis that you can forward to your SIEM engineer? And can we put a placeholder in late January to review results before your planning starts?"
quality_notes: Strong: accepts the budget freeze, asks when budget reopens and what the CFO will need, and proposes a no-cost analysis on her noisiest rule so she enters planning with her own evidence. The weak version argued, suggested repurposing other budgets and dangled a threshold-dodging discount.
